name: Silent-Sanctum
geological_features: Stratified cloud bands of metallic hydrogen
specific_features: Anomalous radio silence zone in upper atmosphere
Stable equatorial cloud formation resembling a closed eye
description: Silent-Sanctum is a brooding gas giant wrapped in bands of deep indigo and charcoal gray, its atmosphere notably darker than most worlds of its class. The planet spans sixty-two thousand kilometers at its equator, its massive gravitational pull shepherding a system of icy moons and captured asteroids into orderly orbits. Deep within the atmosphere, pressures compress hydrogen into metallic states and carbon into crystalline structures that will never see the light of any star.

The most unsettling feature of Silent-Sanctum is the dead zone in its upper atmosphere, a region spanning thousands of kilometers where all electromagnetic signals simply cease. Ships passing through experience complete communications blackout, their instruments reading nothing but silence across every frequency. The stable cloud formation at the equator, which survey teams have named the Closed Eye, sits at the center of this dead zone like a pupil in a vast, sleeping face.

Three expeditions have sent atmospheric probes into the dead zone, and all three lost contact with their instruments at precisely the same depth. The probes were never recovered, and telemetry up to the cutoff point showed no anomalous conditions that would explain the signal loss. Theories range from exotic electromagnetic absorption by unusual atmospheric chemistry to more speculative proposals that the planet's magnetic field creates a natural Faraday cage of unprecedented scale.

Silent-Sanctum's helium-3 reserves are substantial enough to fuel a sector's worth of fusion reactors for centuries, but harvesting operations must contend with the dead zone and the unpredictable behavior of equipment within it. Two fuel-skimming corporations have established orbital platforms outside the zone's influence, dipping collection arrays into the upper atmosphere at carefully plotted angles. The profit margins are enormous, but so is the insurance cost, and the Closed Eye watches every operation with what the crews insist is patient, deliberate attention.
